articles.content: Economic and event calendar in Asia 03 November 2026 - RBA rate hike expected Apple and Palantir earnings preview: The numbers buyers and sellers will be watching Iran and US reportedly on verge of preliminary agreement Gold Technicals: Gold is up sharply erasing some of last week's declines. Bounces off key MA target. US construction spending for the month of September -1.9% versus 0.3% estimate US ISM manufacturing PMI for October 55.5 versus 54.5 estimate US S&P Global final manufacturing PMI for October 54.9 vs 56.0 preliminary Canada S&P global manufacturing PMI 49.6 versus 51.5 last month US election: The key races that could tip control of Congress Iran’s Pezeshkian says Supreme Leader has granted government some authority on dialogue Morning Kickstart: Oil tumbles as Iran talks continue. USD mixed ahead of ISM investingLive European session wrap: Oil sinks, stocks steady as US midterm elections loom November started with hopes for a rebound after a difficult October. By the afternoon, however, sellers were back in control of technology shares. Optimism surrounding US–Iran diplomacy helped send crude oil sharply lower, but that potential positive for inflation and business costs was not enough to sustain the early stock-market gains. The divergence is the story. The Dow is holding higher, while the S&P and Nasdaq indices are falling. Treasury yields are mostly lower, gold and silver are rebounding, and Bitcoin is struggling alongside technology shares. Buyers found some relief from lower oil, but confidence in the AI trade remains under pressure. Dollar mixed as the Swiss franc leads The USD is mixed in the supplied afternoon snapshot, with its largest decline against the Swiss franc and its strongest gain against the Australian dollar. EURUSD is up 0.33% at 1.1195, while GBPUSD has gained 0.13% to 1.3409. USDCHF is down 0.87% at 0.8178, highlighting the franc’s relative strength. Meanwhile, USDJPY is up 0.22% at 157.88 and USDCAD is 0.09% higher at 1.3986. The AUDUSD is down 0.46% at 0.6998, while NZDUSD has slipped 0.18% to 0.5618. That combination is consistent with a more cautious tone as the equity rebound fades. Treasury yields mostly lower Longer-dated Treasury yields are moving lower, while the 2-year is little changed. The afternoon levels show: 2-year: 4.5833%, up 0.23 basis points. 5-year: 4.6931%, down 2.89 basis points. 10-year: 4.8960%, down 3.30 basis points. 30-year: 5.2751%, down 3.39 basis points. The sharp fall in crude offers some relief on future inflation pressures, while weaker construction spending and renewed equity selling provide additional reasons for demand for bonds. However, the manufacturing reports still point to uncomfortable price pressures. The data do not give the Fed an uncomplicated signal to ease. Dow holds higher as technology retreats The supplied afternoon index changes show: Dow industrial average: +0.52%. S&P 500: −0.41%. Nasdaq Composite: −0.96%. Nasdaq 100: −1.29%. The larger decline in the Nasdaq 100 underscores the pressure on major growth shares. Lower yields would normally provide some support for those stocks. Today, that support is being overwhelmed by renewed selling. Beneath the indices, the moves are considerably larger. Marvell is down 12.81%, Astera Labs has fallen 11.39%, Intel is off another 8.70%, and AMD is down 7.03%. The weakness extends beyond semiconductors: CoreWeave is down 9.01%, Nebius has fallen 8.20%, Western Digital is off 7.85%, and Datadog is down 7.81%. The common theme is exposure to AI infrastructure, computing, storage and cloud spending. Intel’s continued decline adds to the damage following last week’s earnings selloff. The broad indices tell only part of the story; the repricing underneath remains much more severe. ISM strengthens, but inflation remains elevated The ISM manufacturing report provided the strongest growth signal. October’s headline index rose to 55.5 from 54.5, beating the 54.5 consensus reported in the release. Production increased to 59.0 from 56.7, while new orders edged higher to 55.5 from 55.3. Employment slipped to 52.4 from 52.7 but remained above the 50 expansion barometer. Prices paid eased to 75.2 from 77.9, below the 77.5 estimate. That is encouraging at the margin, but it still signals widespread input-cost increases. Supplier deliveries also slowed slightly further. Manufacturing is expanding, but the improvement comes with supply constraints and elevated costs that keep the Fed cautious. investinglive.com S&P Global PMI shows slower growth and rising costs The final S&P Global manufacturing PMI delivered a less encouraging growth reading. The index was revised down to 54.9 from the preliminary 56.0 and was below September’s 55.9. It remained comfortably above 50, but new-order growth slowed to its weakest since March. Employment growth was the strongest since April 2021, while selling prices increased at their fastest pace since September 2022. Delivery times also lengthened sharply. For companies, the message is mixed: activity continues to expand, but higher costs and supply delays create pressure on margins. investinglive.com Construction spending is the clear weak spot September construction spending fell 1.9%, compared with expectations for a 0.3% increase. August was revised higher to +2.0% from +0.9%, which cushions the monthly comparison, but the underlying weakness remains evident. Private residential spending dropped 5.5%, outweighing a 1.1% increase in private nonresidential construction. Total spending was down 2.7% from a year earlier and 2.9% through the first nine months of 2026. Taken together, the US reports show an uneven economy. Manufacturing continues to grow, but housing-related construction is weakening and inflation pressures remain elevated. That combination offers neither a clean growth story for stocks nor a clear easing signal for the Fed. investinglive.com Canada’s manufacturing report was weaker still. Its PMI fell to 49.6 from 51.5, slipping into contraction as output, orders and employment declined. Rising input costs and selling prices added an uncomfortable inflation element to the slowdown. investinglive.com Crude plunges on diplomacy hopes WTI crude is trading at $96.12, down $8.00 or 7.68% in the supplied snapshot. InvestingLive’s coverage highlighted hopes that negotiations could produce a framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. However, the reported Iranian proposal remained conditional, and Washington had not accepted it. The market is pricing greater hope for progress, while a completed agreement remains outstanding. investinglive.com Lower oil could ease pressure on consumers, transportation costs and inflation. The failure of technology shares to hold their rebound despite that relief shows how persistent the selling has become. Gold and silver rebound; Bitcoin slips Spot gold is trading near $3,942.77, up about $67 or 1.73%. Silver is up 2.77% at $50.47. Gold’s advance is consistent with lower Treasury yields, which reduce the opportunity cost of holding a metal that pays no interest. The dollar’s mixed performance also leaves gold without a uniform currency headwind. Silver is participating in the metals rebound despite the more cautious equity backdrop. Bitcoin is moving in the opposite direction, down 1.84% at $76,795. For this session, it is behaving more like the pressured technology trade than the recovering precious-metals market. The next test is whether lower oil and yields can eventually help buyers stabilize stocks, or whether AI selling continues to dominate. Apple and Palantir earnings after the close, followed by Tuesday’s US midterm elections, keep traders focused on both corporate expectations and policy uncertainty. This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Supermarket freezers in several European countries hit by apparent cyberattacks
articles.desc: Some of the stores affected were forced to discard spoiled food.
articles.content: Supermarket freezers in several European countries hit by apparent cyberattacks | United States Supermarket freezers in several European countries hit by apparent cyberattacks Some of the stores affected were forced to discard spoiled food. Trinity AudioSTOCKHOLM — Supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland and Estonia were hit Monday by problems with freezers and fridges that apparently were caused by cyberattacks, forcing some to dispose of ruined food.in which attackers remotely took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, sending temperatures soaring. Gustaf Nilsson, a spokesperson for Sweden’s ICA Group supermarket chain, told the TT news agency that “a limited number” of stores were affected overnight by an incident that affected refrigeration and freezing systems. He declined to give a specific number. An ICA Kvantum store in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, said its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius . In a Facebook post, it said staff were discarding affected products. Cyberattack on Swedish Supermarket Freezers Follows France Attack The Coop chain said that six of its stores in central Sweden had problems with their fridges and freezers, TT reported, though it didn’t immediately have details. The Delhaize chain said that an “IT incident” had affected refrigeration systems in several dozen of its stores, mostly in Belgium but also a few in neighboring Luxembourg. Destroyed refrigerated goods are being thrown away from powerless freezers at ICA Baronen store on Odengatan in Stockholm, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, as some of stores have suffered problems with their refrigerators and freezers overnight. “In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centers are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores,” spokesperson Sarah De Meester said. Carrefour said a cyberattack targeting refrigeration systems had affected 15 of its more than 700 stores in Belgium, describing the impact as “extremely limited. ” In Estonia, a refrigeration technology company said attackers had accessed a computer controlling a client’s refrigeration system and raised the temperature to 50 degrees Celsius, public broadcaster ERR reported. Jann Mutso, chief executive of Kitman Coldtech, declined to identify the store but said the attack was addressed within minutes and caused no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets was affected. In Ireland, 13 SuperValu stores were affected, The Irish Times reported. A spokesperson for Musgrave Group, which owns SuperValu, told the newspaper that chilled and frozen products had been removed from sale as a precaution.appeared to target old systems. articles.title: Telangana Indiramma Towers: E-lottery for flats in four constituencies on November
articles.desc: Telangana Housing Board to conduct e-lottery for Indiramma Towers flats in four constituencies on November 3 and a mop-up lottery for vacant flats on November 4.
articles.content: Telangana Indiramma Towers: E-lottery for flats in four constituencies on November The Telangana Housing Board will conduct online lotteries on November 3 and 4 for allotment of flats under the , covering fresh beneficiaries in four Assembly constituencies and vacant flats in previously allotted segments. Housing Board Vice-Chairman V.P. Gautam said an e-lottery would be held on November 3 to select eligible beneficiaries from Musheerabad, LB Nagar, Chandrayangutta and Goshamahal constituencies. The preliminary scrutiny of applications received from these constituencies has been completed, and the online lottery will ensure transparent selection. A mop-up lottery will be conducted on November 4 to allot flats that became vacant following the cancellation of some earlier allotments in 16 Assembly constituencies. The cancellations were made for various reasons, including beneficiaries already owning houses, failure to deposit the prescribed Rs.1 lakh within the stipulated period and applicants not residing in the respective Assembly constituencies. The vacant flats will be allotted to other eligible applicants who had already submitted their applications. Gautam said both lottery processes would be conducted online in a transparent manner and telecast live on the Housing Department’s YouTube channel and other social media platforms. Applicants were mapped to their respective Assembly constituencies using geocoding based on residential addresses and Google Maps. In Thiruvananthapuram district, as many as 42 road works in rural local bodies did not have any takers despite being tendered thrice. The rates of Bitumen went up due to the war situation in West Asia. Considering the rising cost of building materials, the department had from May 2025 made effective a new schedule of rates as well as allowed tender excess of up to 10%. Minister for Local Self Governments K.M.Shaji had last week said in the Assembly that the department is now considering a proposal of the Chief Engineer to permit excess costs in similar lines to the Public Works department’s order issued earlier. Contractors who regularly take up work under local bodies have been demanding a similar order for the past few months. Some of the major road works in rural Thiruvananthapuram, proposed to be taken up under the various panchayats as well as the Thiruvananthapuram district panchayat and some block panchayats have been pending for quite some time. articles.title: Pupils miss exam as transport drivers down tools over alleged R450m bill
articles.content: Pupils miss exam as transport drivers down tools over alleged R450m bill Pupils miss exam as transport drivers down tools over alleged R450m bill The pupils come from disadvantaged families Hundreds of Gauteng pupils who depend on scholar transport missed the Life Orientation exam on Monday after their drivers abruptly downed tools, leaving them stranded. The pupils come from disadvantaged families and are assisted to and from school by buses paid for by the government. However, the government has allegedly failed to pay the bus operators for the past three months, resulting in the pupils being unable to make it to school for their exams. Among those affected were 653 pupils from A parent who spoke to Sowetan on condition of anonymity said the absence of transport on Monday led to their children missing a Life Orientation (LO) exam. “The learners in grades 8, 9 and 10 today were meant to be writing their first paper of LO. The exam has been postponed to Tuesday when transport is available,” she said. Jabulani Khumalo, chairperson of the Gauteng Small Bus Operators Council, told Sowetan they had services because the provincial education department owed them an estimated amount of more than R450m. He said more than 2,000 vehicles were transporting pupils throughout the province to different schools. “Per month, the invoice is about R150m. We have not been paid in 90 days. This means we also can’t meet our financial obligations to pay business suppliers, employees, and our creditors, including the banks. We have not received any price increases on this job since 2022. Suppliers now don’t want to give us anything on credit, making it difficult to run a business “Interest accumulates, and when they eventually pay, the money falls short, and our credit scores are affected. We have to approach loan sharks.” Khumalo said non-payment was so serious that some operators were having their assets repossessed, while others were sick with stress. In addition, he said, fuel prices, particularly diesel, had added to the crisis. “In February it was around R19, and now it is almost double that. We can’t keep up because the government has not subsidised us for fuel. “We have not received any price increases on this job since 2022. Suppliers now don’t want to give us anything on credit, making it difficult to run a business.” According to Khumalo, an emergency meeting was held on Monday with the Gauteng government to determine a way forward. As a result, He said they had met with the Gauteng department of education, the treasury, and the premier’s office to discuss the matter. “There’s a commitment by the premier that August and September invoices will be processed from Thursday, November 5, and other grievances will be addressed in the meeting scheduled for November 11 2026.” Southern African Bus Operators’ Association spokesperson Tumi Mashiane said while most of their buses don’t do scholar transport, they are aware of the challenge their counterparts are facing. “It’s not just August and September that scholar transport operators have not been paid. Some haven’t been paid since May and June. It is really a challenge.” Sowetan sent a media enquiry to the Gauteng department of education seeking clarity on the reported non-payment, the affected transport providers and the number of pupils who had been affected. The department acknowledged receipt of the enquiry and committed to respond. However, a response had not yet been received at the time of publication. articles.title: AI Productivity Starts With Redesigning the Work | Opinion
articles.desc: AI may boost productivity, but companies risk scaling it before redesigning processes, governance and decision-making authority.
articles.content: AI Productivity Starts With Redesigning the Work | Opinion - Newsweek Global organizations are making a dangerous bet. Companies are restructuring their workforces around AI productivity gains while many have yet to build the operating models needed to deliver them. The gap between technological ambition and operational readiness is substantial. According to SSON Research & Analytics’ 2026 research, digitalization is a leading Global Business Services (GBS) priority, yet fewer than one in five organizations have automated the majority of their processes. Legacy technology remains the leading barrier to transformation. The message for executives is uncomfortable: the technology race is advancing faster than the organizational changes required to make it pay off. I believe this is one of the most consequential management challenges of the AI era. Companies are investing in technology capable of coordinating work across entire business processes while retaining structures built around departmental expertise. They expect AI to eliminate inefficiencies that their own operating models continue to create. More concerningly, some are beginning to make workforce decisions based on productivity gains that have yet to materialize. Consider order-to-cash, the process that takes a customer from initial setup to completed payment. Sales takes the order, supply chain fulfills it, and finance issues the invoice and collects the money. Each department may meet its performance targets, yet the customer can still experience delays, errors, and frustration. Every handoff introduces another opportunity for the process to break down. This is how an enterprise can have green dashboards across its departments and a failing business process overall. The fundamental problem is that companies are organized around expertise rather than outcomes. The problem is not a lack of awareness. Companies have appointed Global Process Owners (GPOs) for years, recognizing the need to coordinate work across traditional functional boundaries. Yet these leaders are frequently expected to influence decisions without possessing the authority to make them. An adviser can recommend a better process. An accountable owner can deliver one. A Critical Distinction SSON Research & Analytics found that 90 percent of organizations with GPOs reported a positive impact on process performance. That is an encouraging signal, but the same research identifies a critical distinction between having a process owner on the organizational chart and giving that person the authority to change how the work gets done. A title cannot resolve competing departmental priorities. Decision rights can. AI makes this structural weakness more consequential. Who determines which decisions an AI agent can make? Who resolves conflicting data standards? Who decides which systems are redundant? If authority is fragmented, every answer becomes a negotiation. The technology encounters the same organizational bottlenecks that have slowed transformation for years. That gap becomes dangerous when projected AI efficiencies begin driving workforce decisions. Companies may reduce headcount before the processes and capabilities needed to absorb that work are actually in place. Employees can lose their jobs before the technology is ready to assume their responsibilities, leaving the remaining workforce to manage the resulting failures and backlogs. The Consequences The consequences extend into everyday life. Customers wait longer for services, employees inherit poorly designed workflows, and businesses pay for technology that underdelivers. Properly implemented AI within an evolved operating model could free people from repetitive administration and give them more time for problem-solving and customer engagement. Implementing AI without thinking through the operating model could leave organizations understaffed, operationally fragile, and unable to meet the expectations they have created. articles.title: The Latinx Center at The University of Denver
articles.content: The Latinx Center at The University of Denver Advancing the legacies of Latinx communities The Latinx Center at The University of Denver advances critical interdisciplinary research, scholarly and creative work, and curricular development related to the historical, political, cultural, and intellectual legacy of Latinx people. The Latinx Center promotes excellence in scholarship and teaching to reflect the cultural experiences of Latinx people across the globe. Through its varied scholarly and cultural activities and events, the center promotes a vision rooted in social justice and equity and is an essential participant in a cultural and intellectual process of empowerment and transformation. By investing in people who are traditionally excluded, we create a scholarship for and by Latinx communities, advancing knowledge of our history, politics, culture, and legacies. As a community of scholars, we center the connection between the mind and the heart of the community which is the foundation from which we have emerged as scholars. The Latinx Center plays a critical role in the creation and dissemination of knowledge and understanding about the Latinx experience. We promote a liberative critical engagement of the scholarship, pedagogy, university and society that surrounds us. Critical inquiry that incorporates the rich histories of Latinx communities. Publications, events and engagement pertaining to the Latinx community. Grant funding for students and community leadership opportunities. The Latinx Center provides mentorship, funding and support for Latinx graduate students and faculty, and those engaging in research and creative works focused on the Latinx experience. We center the needs of Latinx students and faculty, and further our impact with regards to Latinx issues, concerns, and communities, domestic and international.

articles.content: The Chang’e-6 mission has uncovered crucial insights into the Moon's internal chemistry based on basalt samples. It was found that these samples contained heavier potassium isotopes than those from previous Apollo and Chang’e-5 missions. This evidence points to a significant ancient impact that may have altered deep material within the Moon's mantle, potentially leading to potassium evaporation that influences its signature.
